endorsements.title: A Prompt Engineering Framework for Large Language Model-Based Mental Health Chatbots: Conceptual Framework
endorsements.quote: This filter checks for compassionate language, the absence of derogatory or overly commanding speech, and the exclusion of banned content, such as information on lethal means or others’ personal identifying information.

evidence.title: PAIR-SAFE: A Paired-Agent Approach for Runtime Auditing and Refining AI-Mediated Mental Health Support
evidence.outcome: MITI-4 dimension scores with vs without Judge-agent runtime auditing (ALLOW/REVISE) of mental health responses
evidence.effect: Judge-supervised interactions showed significant improvements in Partnership, Seek Collaboration, and overall Relational quality; specific numbers not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We find that Judge-supervised interactions show significant improvements in key MITI dimensions, including Partnership, Seek Collaboration, and overall Relational quality.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Correctness and Diversity in Synthetic Dialogues
evidence.outcome: error rates and harmful responses with automated safety filtering
evidence.effect: safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses
evidence.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic patient-AI Coach dialogues (250 per model x 5 models)

evidence.title: Safe Deployment of a Generative AI Assistant for Traditional-Medicine Education: Defense-in-Depth Architecture, Domain-Calibrated Safety Evaluation, and a Proposed Minimum Safety Stack
evidence.outcome: harmful or unsafe responses under attacks
evidence.effect: Defense-in-depth TLAS-YHCT achieved 100% safe-response rate across 206 attacks.
evidence.quote: A structured red-team of 206 attacks—constructed by domain-expert clinician-educators independent of system developers, scored blind by the same experts under a dual IT-security and clinical-education safety criterion—yielded a 100% safe-response rate versus 88.9% and 78.7% for two commercial baselines.

evidence.title: A cross-sectional evaluation of Large Language Model answers to dental questions
evidence.outcome: Harmful answer rate with vs without safety-oriented system prompt
evidence.effect: Without a system prompt 56% of outputs were harmful; a safety-oriented system prompt reduced this by 26 percentage points to 30%.
evidence.quote: A safety-oriented system prompt reduced this rate by 26 percentage points to 30%.

evidence.title: Correctness, Harmfulness, and Diversity of Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic dialogues per model (50 per model human-rated)

evidence.title: Preventing Another Tessa: Modular Safety Middleware For Health-Adjacent AI Assistants
evidence.effect: achieved perfect interception of unsafe prompts at baseline cost and latency, outperforming traditional multi-stage pipelines
evidence.quote: Using synthetic evaluations, we show that this design achieves perfect interception of unsafe prompts at baseline cost and latency, outperforming traditional multi-stage pipelines.

evidence.title: Improving the Safety and Trustworthiness of Medical AI via Multi-Agent Evaluation Loops
evidence.outcome: Ethical violations and risk level of LLM responses after iterative automated evaluator-agent review
evidence.effect: Iterative multi-agent loop achieved an 89% reduction in ethical violations and a 92% risk downgrade rate across 900 queries.
evidence.quote: The iterative multi-agent loop achieved an 89% reduction in ethical violations and a 92% risk downgrade rate, underscoring the effectiveness of our approach.

evidence.title: MindGuard: Guardrail Classifiers for Multi-Turn Mental Health Support
evidence.effect: Lower attack success and harmful engagement rates in adversarial multi-turn interactions than general-purpose safeguards.
evidence.quote: Our classifiers reduce false positives at high-recall operating points and, when paired with clinician language models, help achieve lower attack success and harmful engagement rates in adversarial multi-turn interactions compared to general-purpose safeguards.

evidence.title: ExpGuard: LLM Content Moderation in Specialized Domains
evidence.outcome: Guardrail model classification of harmful prompts and responses in finance, medical, legal domains under adversarial attack
evidence.effect: ExpGuard surpassed WildGuard by up to 8.9% in prompt classification and 15.3% in response classification, with competitive performance on eight public benchmarks and resilience to domain-specific adversarial attacks.
evidence.quote: Comprehensive evaluations conducted on ExpGuardTest and eight established public benchmarks reveal that ExpGuard delivers competitive performance across the board while demonstrating exceptional resilience to domain-specific adversarial attacks, surpassing state-of-the-art models such as WildGuard by up to 8.9% in prompt classification and 15.3% in response classification.
evidence.sample_unit: labeled prompts (with paired refusal and compliant responses) in ExpGuardMix

evidence.title: CareGuardAI: Context-Aware Multi-Agent Guardrails for Clinical Safety & Hallucination Mitigation in Patient-Facing LLMs
evidence.outcome: Safety and hallucination detection on PatientSafeBench, MedSafetyBench, and MedHallu with a pre-release risk gate versus baselines
evidence.effect: Framework releasing responses only when SRA and HRA are <=2 consistently outperformed strong baseline models including GPT-4o-mini; no numeric results in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Across these benchmarks, the framework consistently outperforms strong baseline models, including GPT-4o-mini, demonstrating the importance of context-aware, risk-based, inference-time safety mechanisms for reliable deployment in healthcare.

evidence.title: DrugBench: Evaluating AI Control Protocols for Medication Harm Mitigation
evidence.outcome: Whether AI control protocols mitigate medication-harm outputs and resist subversion
evidence.effect: Existing control protocols can be subverted under a severity-based safety definition; severity-based monitoring is proposed to address this. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Under this revised definition, we show that existing control protocols can be subverted and propose severity-based monitoring to address this limitation.

evidence.title: Standard guardrails impose a safety-critical omission tax on clinical large language models that a downstream verification layer reverses: a retrospective multi-cohort evaluation
evidence.outcome: Commission and safety-critical omission with a standard four-component guardrail stack versus bare model
evidence.effect: The guardrail stack lowered commission but raised safety-critical omission by 12.5 percentage points across 921 paired case-runs (17.6% to 30.1%).
evidence.quote: In a retrospective, pre-specified evaluation of three frontier large language models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7) on a contamination-excluded corpus of 1,363 clinical cases, a standard four-component guardrail stack lowered commission but raised safety-critical omission by 12.5 percentage points across 921 paired case-runs (17.6% to 30.1%).

evidence.title: Development and evaluation of an agentic LLM based RAG framework for evidence-based patient education
evidence.outcome: LLM validation agent blocking of harmful generated PEMs
evidence.effect: Accuracy 0.40-0.82 across 12 LLMs; only models ≥27B exceeded 0.80; even top performers failed to dependably block category 3 unscientific advice.
evidence.quote: It is noteworthy that the full results from the VA evaluation ( online supplemental results , sheet ‘VA Eval’) show that even the top performers failed to dependably block harmful PEMs belonging to category 3 (unscientific or time-wasting medical advice).
evidence.sample_unit: patient education questions (12 LLMs x 4 setups); 50 PEMs for validation agent test

evidence.title: Health Disinformation Use Case Highlighting the Urgent Need for Artificial Intelligence Vigilance: Weapons of Mass Disinformation
evidence.outcome: Ability of LLM guardrails to block generation of harmful health disinformation
evidence.effect: 102 distinct disinformation blog articles (>17,000 words) on vaccines and vaping generated in 65 minutes, plus 20 realistic images in under 2 minutes, without specialized knowledge in bypassing guardrails.
evidence.quote: These observations demonstrate that when the guardrails of AI tools are insufficient, the ability to rapidly generate diverse and large amounts of convincing disinformation is profound.

evidence.title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
evidence.outcome: Content filters blocking harmful generated outputs and resistance to circumvention
evidence.effect: Claude 2 declined all 130 prompts even with jailbreaking; Copilot blocked initially but not at 12 weeks; ChatGPT, Bard, HuggingChat generated disinformation, 5% refusal (7 of 150).
evidence.quote: Claude 2 (via Poe) declined 130 prompts submitted across the two study timepoints requesting the generation of content claiming that sunscreen causes skin cancer or that the alkaline diet is a cure for cancer, even with jailbreaking attempts.

evidence.title: Development and Evaluation of an Augmented Artificial Intelligence Model for Urogynecology Queries
evidence.quote: All responses were additionally screened for potentially harmful, biased, or misleading content, and none was identified.

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen simulated or benchmark studies suggest that automated pre-delivery filters and judge agents may reduce harmful generated output, but several found that harm persisted and one found that a guardrail stack increased omission of safety-relevant information. No study tested filtering of copyright-infringing or unlawful content, and none was conducted with live patients.

perspectives.view: All 13 tests used synthetic dialogues, vignettes, or automated benchmarks, and none measured patient outcomes. Eight reported support and five reported null or mixed results. Many abstracts gave no numbers. Certainty is very low because of indirectness, inconsistency across models and designs, and imprecision.

In one benchmark, a four-component guardrail stack lowered commission errors but raised omission of safety-relevant information from 17.6% to 30.1%. A safety filter cut harmful output for Mistral from 13.1% to 4.4% but changed GPT-4.1 only from 9/250 to 8/250. These results suggest filters may shift harm rather than remove it.

Resistance to circumvention varied. One defense-in-depth system gave safe responses to all 206 attacks, while another study found existing control protocols could be subverted. In a hazard study, Copilot blocked disinformation prompts initially but not at 12 weeks, which suggests one-time testing may not hold as models change.

One benchmark reported full interception of unsafe prompts at baseline cost and latency. A validation-agent study found accuracy of 0.40 to 0.82 across 12 models, and only models of 27B parameters or larger exceeded 0.80. This suggests that dependable checking may require larger models and the compute costs that come with them.

Two tests included non-English or limited English proficiency content. A safety-oriented system prompt lowered harmful answers from 56% to 30%, though a system prompt differs from a post-generation filter. A validation agent in Qatar did not dependably block unscientific advice. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

NIST AI 600-1, the CHAI guide, and one commentary endorse output checks. No supplied study tested whether filters block copyright-infringing or otherwise unlawful content, so that part of the recommendation rests on endorsement alone.

The rise in omitted safety information under a guardrail stack means a filtered answer can leave patients without warnings they need. No study measured what patients see when output is blocked or whether they are directed to a human.

commentary.research_gap: Prospective evaluations in live clinical or patient-facing deployments should measure harmful output, omission of needed safety information, and false blocking together, repeat circumvention testing over time as models update, and include tests of copyright and legal-compliance filtering, which no current study addresses.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included non-English or limited English proficiency content, one in Qatar, and neither was run with real patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so performance of these filters for those users is unknown.
